subject: Origen (Origen of Alexandria). Church Father. Not counted a saint.
texts_on_disk: design/saints-hub/sources/people/origen/ (gitignored). raw-*.txt are whole CCEL volumes; the named .txt files are the works or chapters cut from them, or stripped web pages (first line URL). text_used.text: Quotations are word for word from public-domain translations: A. C. McGiffert's Eusebius (NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890); Frederick Crombie's Origen (ANF vol. 4, 1885); Allan Menzies's Origen (ANF vol. 9, 1896); S. D. F. Salmond's Gregory Thaumaturgus (ANF vol. 6, 1886); W. H. Fremantle's Jerome and Rufinus (NPNF 2nd series vols. 3 and 6, 1892-1893); E. C. Richardson's Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892); Marcus Dods's Augustine, City of God (NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887); Newman and Robertson's Athanasius (NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892); Browne and Swallow's Gregory of Nazianzus (NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894); H. R. Percival's Fifth Council (NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900); J. H. Freese's Photius (1920, on tertullian.org). The whole CCEL plain-text volumes (marked 'Rights: Public Domain') were downloaded; New Advent's revised copies were also fetched, because the site already links New Advent.
text_used.source: CCEL cache files, e.g. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/s/schaff/npnf201/cache/npnf201.txt, anf04.txt, anf09.txt, anf06.txt, npnf203.txt, npnf206.txt, npnf214.txt, npnf102.txt, npnf204.txt, npnf207.txt
text_used.note: Differences between CCEL and New Advent that matter: New Advent spells 'defense' where Crombie's CCEL text has 'defence' (the site's 'dreams' line uses New Advent's 'defense'). New Advent numbers Gregory Thaumaturgus's Panegyric in 19 'Arguments'; CCEL in 18. On First Principles Book 4 appears twice on New Advent: 'Translated from the Latin of Rufinus' and 'Translated from the Greek' (of the Philocalia). Lines quoted from Book 4 below are from the GREEK section, which is Origen's own words; most of the rest of On First Principles survives only in Rufinus's Latin, which Rufinus admitted smoothing. Much of what we have of Origen's letters survives only in Eusebius's Greek or in Jerome's Latin.

born.text: About 185, probably at Alexandria in Egypt (still called Alexandria). His parents were Christians, says Eusebius; the pagan Porphyry claimed otherwise.
born.source: Britannica, 'Origen' ('born c. 185, probably Alexandria, Egypt'; 'born of pagan parents, according to ... Porphyry, but of Christian parents, according to ... Eusebius ... whose account is probably more accurate'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), 'Origen and Origenism' ('Born in 185'); Crombie, ANF 4 introductory note ('born in all probability at Alexandria, about the year 185'). Eusebius, Church History 6.2.2 and 6.2.12: his father died in the persecution of 'the tenth year of the reign of Severus' (202), when Origen was 'not quite seventeen years old'.
born.note: No ancient source names the city of his birth outright; 'probably Alexandria' is the careful wording. Merriam-Webster gives '185?-?254'. Eusebius 6.19.10 answers Porphyry: 'the doctrine of Christ was taught to Origen by his parents'. Crombie adds that his name 'is derived from that of an Egyptian deity' (born of Horus); keep that out unless wanted, it is Crombie's note, not an ancient source.

grew_up.text: At Alexandria. His father Leonides taught him Scripture before Greek learning, making him learn and recite passages every day.
grew_up.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.2.7-8: 'before inducting him into the Greek sciences, he drilled him in sacred studies, requiring him to learn and recite every day.'
grew_up.note: His father's name: 'Leonidas' in Jerome, Lives 54; 'Leonides' in Photius and in the 1916 Roman Martyrology (22 April).

died.text: About 253 or 254, at Tyre (today Sour, or Ṣūr, in Lebanon), aged 69. He had been imprisoned and tortured in the persecution of the emperor Decius (250) and died a few years later. Buried at Tyre.
died.source: Eusebius, Church History 7.1 ('At this time Origen died, being sixty-nine years of age', in the reign of Gallus); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54 ('He lived until the time of Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until his sixty-ninth year, and died at Tyre, in which city he also was buried'); Britannica ('died c. 254, Tyre, Phoenicia [now Ṣūr, Lebanon]'; 'imprisoned and tortured but survived to die several years later'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('probably, from the results of the sufferings endured during the persecution (253 or 254), at the age of sixty-nine').
died.note: Cause: no ancient source says outright that the torture killed him. The Catholic Encyclopedia says 'probably'. Plain wording that holds: 'He died a few years after being tortured for his faith.' No day of death is recorded. Menzies (ANF 9) says 'probably in the year 254'. Eusebius 6.39.5 says his letters written after the torture survived, which is why the Tyre account is preferred (Photius, codex 118).

buried.text: At Tyre. His tomb there was honoured for centuries: in the Crusader period it was shown behind the high altar of the cathedral of Tyre. Its place is now unknown.
buried.source: Jerome, Lives 54 ('died at Tyre, in which city he also was buried'); Britannica ('His tomb at Tyre was held in honour, and its long survival is attested by historians of the period of the Crusades'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('his sepulchre, behind the high-altar of the cathedral of Tyr, was visited by pilgrims ... the exact location of his tomb is unknown').
buried.note: The Crusader-era witnesses themselves (e.g. William of Tyre) were not fetched. Rely on Britannica and the Catholic Encyclopedia for this line.

also_called.text: Adamantius ('man of steel', 'man of adamant'). Eusebius says it was another name of his. Jerome calls him 'our Christian man of brass, or, rather, man of adamant'. Photius heard it was because his arguments were 'linked together like chains of adamant'.
also_called.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.14.10 ('But Adamantius,--for this also was a name of Origen'); Jerome, Letter 33, to Paula, section 3; Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 118 (tr. Freese, 1920)
also_called.note: Photius's explanation is 9th-century hearsay ('He is said to have been also called Adamantius, because his arguments were linked together like chains of adamant'); Jerome's is that his zeal for Scripture 'fairly earned for him this latter name'. Merriam-Webster and Britannica give the full name as 'Oregenes Adamantius'.

also_called.text: Origen of Alexandria. No church gives him a saint's title: never 'St Origen'.
also_called.source: Usage (Britannica, Catholic Encyclopedia); status section below
also_called.note: Search brief: the bare word 'origen' is dominated by Orijen dog food, so titles use 'Origen of Alexandria'.

status.text: Church Father. Not counted a saint by any church we checked: Catholic, Orthodox, Coptic, Anglican, Episcopal or Lutheran. Condemned by name about three centuries after his death. Many who condemned his ideas still admired him, and he died after torture for the faith.
status.note: Catholic technical usage: the Catholic Encyclopedia's 'Fathers of the Church' (1909) says early authors who fail the tests of orthodoxy and holiness are 'simply ecclesiastical writers'. So a strict Catholic reader might object to 'Church Father'. The site's settled wording 'Church Father. Not counted a saint.' is the popular sense; the brief orders it. Consider one plain sentence on the page: 'In strict Catholic usage he is an "ecclesiastical writer", not a Father.'

patron_of.text: None. He is not a saint, so no church names him patron of anything.
patron_of.source: Status section; no patronage in any calendar checked
patron_of.note: Leave the 'Patron of' row out of his sheet.

in_art.text: No church icons, since no church venerates him. Western books show him as an old bearded scholar with books and a scroll (André Thevet's portrait book, 1584), or teaching a crowd of students (Jan Luyken, 1700). A 12th-century Bavarian manuscript shows him as an author. Some late medieval manuscripts show the self-castration Eusebius reports.
in_art.source: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Origen: File:Origen.jpg (Les vrais pourtraits..., 1584), File:OrigenStudentsLuyken.jpg (Luyken, 1700), File:Origen3.jpg (Schäftlarn manuscript, about 1160, BSB Clm 17092, fol. 130v), File:Origen emasculating himself (MS. Douce 195).jpg
in_art.note: Every picture of him is imagined; no likeness survives. Say so in the caption: 'an imagined likeness'.
in_art.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: "no church has an icon of him" is a universal claim nobody checked; dropped from the page.

wrote.text: More than any Christian before him: commentaries on almost every book of the Bible, homilies (sermons), the Hexapla (a six-column Old Testament), On First Principles (four books), Against Celsus (eight books), On Prayer, an Exhortation to Martyrdom, and letters. Most is lost or survives only in Latin translation.
wrote.source: Jerome, Letter 33 ('the labors of this one man have surpassed those of all previous writers, Greek and Latin. Who has ever managed to read all that he has written?'); Eusebius, Church History 6.36.2 ('a work of eight books in answer to ... Celsus'); Catholic Encyclopedia (what survives: two letters, On Prayer, Exhortation to Martyrdom, Contra Celsum in Greek, De principiis in Rufinus's Latin); Britannica (homilies in Latin by Rufinus and Jerome; Hexapla 'a synopsis of six versions')
wrote.note: A count: Jerome says Eusebius's index of Origen's works did not reach 'a third' of six thousand books (Apology against Rufinus 2.22). So 'under 2,000 books' by Jerome's count; the 6,000 figure is Rufinus's report of what Epiphanius claimed to have read, which Jerome calls a falsehood. Ancient 'books' were scroll-length sections, not whole works. Many Greek homilies on the Psalms were found in Munich in 2012 (not fetched here; could_not_verify).
wrote.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: "commentaries on almost every book of the Bible" was not in any source read; page says "commentaries and sermons on much of the Bible" (Britannica: "exposition of the whole Bible").

pronounced.source: Dictionary.com (Random House, American): 'awr-i-jen, -juhn, or-' and Collins (British): '/ˈɒrɪˌdʒɛn/'; Merriam-Webster: 'ˈȯr-ə-jən, ˈär-'
pronounced.note: Collins's own site answered 403; its entry was read on Dictionary.com, which prints it as 'Collins English Dictionary'. Label: 'Pronounced'.
pronounced.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: the page cited only Merriam-Webster, which gives OR-uh-jun. Page now leads with OR-uh-jun, keeps OR-ih-jen (Dictionary.com), and lists Dictionary.com in the sources.

roles.name: Teacher
roles.line: Head of the Alexandrian school at 18
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.3.3 ('He was in his eighteenth year when he took charge of the catechetical school'); Jerome, Lives 54 ('When only eighteen years old')
roles.note: Eusebius 6.3.8: later 'the catechetical school had been entrusted to him alone by Demetrius'.

roles.name: Bible scholar
roles.line: Learned Hebrew; built the six-column Hexapla
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.16.1-4; Britannica ('from c. 212, Origen learned Hebrew and began to compile his Hexapla')

roles.name: Priest
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.23.4 and 6.26; Jerome, Lives 54; Catholic Encyclopedia (231)
roles.note: Britannica dates the Greek journey and ordination 'about 229-230'. Eusebius 6.26 puts his move to Caesarea in 'the tenth year' of Alexander Severus (231/232).

roles.name: Confessor
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.39.5; Catholic Encyclopedia ('He was buried with honour as a confessor of the Faith')
roles.note: 'Confessor' is the ancient word for one who suffered for the faith without being killed. It is a description, not a church title for him; keep it lower-key if it could read like a saint's title.

feast_days.text: None. No church keeps a feast day for Origen. Checked against the churches' own calendars where they could be fetched.

items.text: No feast. He is not in the 1916 Roman Martyrology, which does keep his father, St Leonides (22 April, 'At Alexandria, the birthday of the martyr St. Leonides, who suffered under Severus'), and his martyred pupils Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, Heron, another Serenus and Rhais (Herais) (28 June).
items.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), full text searched (no 'Origen'); entries for 22 April and 28 June read
items.note: Text on disk at sources/people/martin-of-tours/martyrology-1916.txt. The 28 June entry names 'Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, catechumen, Heron, neophyte, another Serenus, Rhais, catechumen, Potamiaena and Marcella'. Eusebius 6.4 names the same pupils. A fine detail for the page: his father and his students are saints; he is not. The current (2004) Martyrology was not checked.

items.text: No feast. The OCA's own pages say the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) examined 'the errors of presbyter Origen' and condemned his teaching on the pre-existence of souls.
items.source: OCA, 'Commemoration of the Holy 165 Fathers of the Fifth Ecumenical Council' (feast 25 July); OCA, The Orthodox Faith vol. III, 'The Fifth Ecumenical Council'
items.note: GOARCH and the Greek synaxaria were not searched for his name (GOARCH blocked the Martin checker). 'No feast' rests on the OCA plus the condemnation.

items.text: No feast. The Coptic Synaxarium honours Pope Demetrius I (12 Baba), and says Demetrius excommunicated 'Aklemos, Origen, and Orianus and others who wrote forbidden books'.
items.source: Coptic Synaxarium, 12 Baba, 'Abba Demetrius I, 12th Pope of Alexandria' (copticchurch.net)
items.note: A Coptic history page (St Mark Coptic diocese wiki, suscopts.org) also says Demetrius's council excommunicated him. Searches for 'is origen a saint in the coptic church' exist (search brief).

items.text: Not in the Common Worship calendar.
items.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar page, text searched (no 'Origen')

items.text: Not in Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022. That book does call him, in its entry for his teacher Clement of Alexandria (5 December), 'the most eminent theologian of early Greek Christianity'.
items.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (PDF, 638 pages, text searched: 3 mentions, none a commemoration)
items.note: Exact: 'His work prepared the way for his pupil Origen, the most eminent theologian of early Greek Christianity.' (Clement's entry).

items.text: Not in the Lutheran Service Book (LCMS) list of commemorations, nor in the ELCA list as Wikipedia gives it.
items.source: Concordia Publishing House, 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations' (LSB pp. xii-xiii); Wikipedia, 'Calendar of saints (Lutheran)'
items.note: ELCA's own Evangelical Lutheran Worship calendar PDF (web.archive.org) answered 429; the ELCA check is through Wikipedia only (could_not_verify).

feast_days.why: He is not venerated anywhere because of the later condemnations (see is_he_a_saint).

lines: Left with his mother and six younger brothers
numbers.note: Exact: 'he was left with his mother and six younger brothers when he was not quite seventeen years old.' Safer to print 'Not quite 17' than 16. Jerome says 'about seventeen'.
'In his eighteenth year' strictly means aged 17. Jerome says 'When only eighteen years old'. Print 18 with Jerome's wording, or '17 or 18'.

lines: Paid for by his friend Ambrose
numbers.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.23.2 ('he dictated to more than seven amanuenses, who relieved each other at appointed times. And he employed no fewer copyists, besides girls who were skilled in elegant writing')

lines: Hebrew and five more versions side by side
Up to nine in the Psalms
numbers.source: Britannica ('The Hexapla was a synopsis of Old Testament versions: the Hebrew and a transliteration, the Septuagint ..., the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion and, for the Psalms, two further translations'); Eusebius, Church History 6.16.3-4 ('after the four prominent translations, he adds not only a fifth, but also a sixth and seventh')
numbers.note: 'Up to nine' is my arithmetic from Britannica (Hebrew, transliteration, four Greek versions, plus up to three more in the Psalms per Eusebius). Safer second line: 'More in the Psalms, one found in a jar'.

lines: Fewer than this, by Jerome's count
numbers.source: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 2.22 ('Count up the index contained in the third volume of Eusebius ... you will not find, I do not say six thousand, but not a third of that number of books')
numbers.note: Chip wording must make 'under' clear, e.g. chip 'Books, by Jerome's count', n 'Under 2,000'.

lines: At Tyre, a few years after torture
numbers.source: Eusebius, Church History 7.1; Jerome, Lives 54 ('until his sixty-ninth year')
numbers.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Jerome says "until his sixty-ninth year", which is not quite "69", so "Eusebius and Jerome agree" is dropped. Page prints Eusebius 7.1: "Sixty-nine years of age" (evidence entry added).

lines: By Eusebius, 'to the number of one hundred'
numbers.note: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'We now possess only two of Origen's letters' (to Gregory and to Africanus) in full. Spare number, use only if six are wanted.

traits.title: on fire from boyhood
traits.text: When his father was arrested, the boy wanted to die with him. His mother begged him, then hid all his clothes to keep him home. So he wrote to his father instead.
traits.exact: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.

traits.title: lived what he taught
traits.text: He sold his library of old books for four obols a day, so he could teach for nothing. For years he slept on the floor, went barefoot and drank no wine. His friends feared for his health. People said of him:
traits.exact: his manner of life was as his doctrine, and his doctrine as his life

traits.title: never stopped reading
traits.text: His friend and patron Ambrose wrote that they never ate a meal together without something being read aloud, and never went to bed before a brother read them Scripture. Jerome, retelling it:
traits.exact: Night and day, in fact, were so ordered that prayer only gave place to reading and reading to prayer.

traits.title: would not curse his enemies
traits.text: His own bishop had him condemned and stripped of his priesthood, and wrote everywhere against him. Origen wrote to friends that he would not answer curse with curse.
traits.exact: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them. For we have been created for blessing, not for cursing.
traits.cite: His letter to friends at Alexandria, as Jerome quotes it in Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, section 18

traits.title: fair to an opponent (spare)
traits.text: At the end of eight books against the pagan Celsus, he asked Ambrose to send him Celsus's promised second book too, so that he could answer it, or:
traits.exact: laying aside all jealousy, we may testify our approval of whatever truth it may contain.

traits.title: brave beside the condemned (spare)
traits.text: In a persecution he stayed with Christians in prison and walked with them to their deaths, kissing them in front of angry crowds. Soldiers were posted round the house where he taught, and he had to move from house to house.
traits.exact: with great boldness saluted the martyrs with a kiss, oftentimes the heathen multitude round about them became infuriated, and were on the point of rushing upon him.

others_on_him.exact: And thus, like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us,--a love at once to the Holy Word, the most lovely object of all, who attracts all irresistibly toward Himself by His unutterable beauty, and to this man, His friend and advocate.
others_on_him.display: And thus, like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us, a love at once to the Holy Word, the most lovely object of all, Who attracts all irresistibly toward Himself by His unutterable beauty, and to this man, His friend and advocate.
others_on_him.who: Gregory Thaumaturgus (the Wonderworker), his pupil for five years, in his farewell speech to Origen
others_on_him.work: Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen
others_on_him.place: Argument 6 (New Advent numbering; the same in CCEL)
others_on_him.note: Tr. S. D. F. Salmond, ANF 6 (1886). The dashes may be dropped for display. Eusebius 6.30: Gregory and his brother stayed 'five years'. Shorter alternative, same speech, Argument 15: 'he was truly a paradise to us after the similitude of the paradise of God'. Authorship of the speech by Gregory is the standard view; a minority of modern scholars doubt it (not checked here). New Advent prints 'within us — a love' (no comma, em dash); CCEL 'within us,--a love'. Otherwise identical.

life_moments.title: The hidden clothes
life_moments.text: Persecution broke out under the emperor Severus, and Origen's father Leonides was arrested. The boy was set on dying with him. His mother begged him, then hid all his clothes so he could not leave the house. He wrote to his father instead, telling him not to give in for the family's sake. Leonides was beheaded. The family's property was seized, and Origen, not quite seventeen, was left with his mother and six younger brothers.
life_moments.note: Beheaded: Eusebius, Church History 6.1 ('Leonides, who was called the father of Origen, and who was beheaded while his son was still young'); checked in eusebius-church-history-book6.txt. The year: 'the tenth year of the reign of Severus' (6.2.2) = 202 (Britannica: 'martyred in the persecution of 202').
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.2.3-5 says a desire for martyrdom seized him; he never says "to die with his father". Page now: "set on being a martyr too". Trait likewise: "longed to die a martyr".

life_moments.title: A teacher at eighteen
life_moments.text: With the other teachers driven out by persecution, pagans came to the young man to learn the faith. In his eighteenth year he was running the city's school for new Christians. He sold his old books for four obols a day and taught for nothing. He fasted, slept on the ground and went barefoot for years.
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.3.9: 'disposed of whatever valuable books of ancient literature he possessed, being satisfied with receiving from the purchaser four oboli a day'; 6.3.12 'never wearing a shoe'.
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.3.3 says "in his eighteenth year" (Jerome says eighteen); the moment cites Eusebius, so the page says "In his eighteenth year". Eusebius 6.3.9 says he sold "whatever valuable books of ancient literature he possessed", not "his library".

life_moments.title: Beside the martyrs
life_moments.text: Several of his first pupils were arrested and killed. He stayed with them in prison and walked with them to execution, kissing them in public. Crowds nearly lynched him. Soldiers were set round the house where he taught, and he had to move from house to house.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 3 and 4
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.4 names Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, Hero, another Serenus and Herais. Luyken's etching (origen-2.jpg) shows soldiers outside the windows while he teaches.
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.3.3-4 says he stood by all the martyrs "whether known to him or strangers", not only his pupils. Page reworded.

life_moments.title: A Bible in six columns
life_moments.text: He learned Hebrew, which few Christians then did. He hunted down every Greek translation of the Old Testament he could find and set them side by side with the Hebrew: the Hexapla. One translation of the Psalms, he said, he found in a jar near Jericho.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 16; Britannica (date and six versions); Jerome, Lives 54 ('contrary to the spirit of his time, and of his people, he learned the Hebrew language')
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.16.3: 'He states of one of these that he found it in a jar in Jericho in the time of Antoninus, the son of Severus' (Caracalla, 211-217). Britannica says 'in a jar in the Jordan Valley'. Keep 'near Jericho'.
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.16.1 says he sought out other translations, some "concealed from remote times"; not "every Greek translation he could find". Page reworded.

life_moments.title: Summoned by the empress-mother
life_moments.text: His fame reached Mammaea, the emperor's mother. She was staying at Antioch, and she sent soldiers to bring him to her. He stayed a while, taught her about Christ, and hurried back to his work.
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.21.4: 'she sent for him with a military escort'. Eusebius places it after Alexander became emperor (222); the Catholic Encyclopedia says 'Towards 218, it would appear'. Print 'about 230' only with a source; 'when Alexander was emperor' is safest.
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.21.4 says "a military escort", not soldiers sent to bring him. Page reworded.

life_moments.title: Ordained, then driven out
life_moments.text: On a church journey to Greece he passed through Palestine, and the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem ordained him a priest. His own bishop, Demetrius, was furious. Two councils at Alexandria banished him and deposed him. He moved to Caesarea for good and opened a new school there. Jerome says he was condemned not for his teaching but because men 'could not tolerate' his eloquence.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 8, 23 and 26; Jerome, Lives 54 ('he offended Demetrius, who was so wildly enraged at him that he wrote everywhere to injure his reputation'); Jerome, Letter 33, section 4; Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 118 (the two decisions, from Pamphilus's Defence)
life_moments.note: Photius (from Pamphilus): the synod decided 'he must not remain in Alexandria or teach there, but that he should be allowed to retain his priesthood', then Demetrius and some Egyptian bishops 'also deprived him of his sacred office'. Eusebius 6.8.4-5 says Demetrius used the self-castration against him. Heraclas, his old pupil, took over the Alexandrian school and then became bishop (6.26).
life_moments.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: date now "About 230". Eusebius 6.23.3-4 puts the ordination after Pontianus became bishop of Rome (230); Britannica says about 229-230; the move to Caesarea is 231 (Eusebius 6.26). Photius, codex 118, does not say the first synod met at Alexandria: it ruled he "must not remain in Alexandria or teach there". Page: "A council of bishops ordered him out of Alexandria".

life_moments.title: Tortured, and kept alive
life_moments.text: In the persecution of Decius he was chained, thrown in a dungeon and fitted with an iron collar. For days his legs were stretched in the stocks. He was threatened with fire. His judge worked hard not to let him die, so there would be no martyr. He survived, wrote letters of comfort, and died a few years later at Tyre, aged sixty-nine.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 39, and Book 7, chapter 1; Jerome, Lives 54
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.39.5, exact: 'bonds and bodily tortures and torments under the iron collar and in the dungeon; and how for many days with his feet stretched four spaces in the stocks he bore patiently the threats of fire'; 'his judge strove eagerly with all his might not to end his life'. Where he was held is not stated (Caesarea is likely but unsourced here); the heading place could be 'Palestine'.

miracles.text: None recorded. Eusebius, Jerome, Gregory Thaumaturgus and Photius tell no wonders worked by Origen. Leave the miracles section out of his page.
miracles.source: Eusebius, Church History Book 6 (read whole); Jerome, Lives 54; Panegyric; Photius codex 118
miracles.note: Eusebius twice says God's providence rescued him from mobs (6.3.5, 'he escaped absolutely and marvelously'), but tells it as protection, not a miracle he worked. His pupil Gregory is the one called the Wonderworker. Origen himself testifies to miracles in his day (Against Celsus 1.46): that belongs in 'Where he stood', not here.

framing.text: Much of Origen is lost. Of what survives, some is in his own Greek, and much only in Latin translations by Rufinus and Jerome, who both edited as they went. Each line below says where it comes from.
framing.source: Britannica (Rufinus's 'Latin paraphrase (which avowedly rewrites heterodox-sounding passages)'); Catholic Encyclopedia

feature.exact: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them. For we have been created for blessing, not for cursing.
feature.display: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them. For we have been created for blessing, not for cursing.
feature.kicker: After his own bishop condemned him
feature.ctx: From a letter to friends at Alexandria, about the bishops who had cast him out. The Greek is lost; it survives because Jerome quoted it in Latin, to accuse his rival Rufinus of cutting it.
feature.work: Letter to friends at Alexandria, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus
feature.source: W. H. Fremantle, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3 (1892)
feature.note: Original language not given: Jerome's Latin was not fetched. Alternative feature with Greek surviving: Against Celsus 8.72 ('stronger than all the evils in the soul is the Word').

lines.exact: For stronger than all the evils in the soul is the Word, and the healing power that dwells in Him; and this healing He applies, according to the will of God, to every man.
lines.display: For stronger than all the evils in the soul is the Word, and the healing power that dwells in Him; and this healing He applies, according to the will of God, to every man.
lines.ctx: His great hope, written late in life against the pagan Celsus. The same chapter leaves open 'whether it shall be so destroyed that it can never anywhere arise again'.

lines.exact: We may therefore make bold to say that the Gospels are the first fruits of all the Scriptures, but that of the Gospels that of John is the first fruits. No one can apprehend the meaning of it except he have lain on Jesus' breast and received from Jesus Mary to be his mother also.
lines.display: We may therefore make bold to say that the Gospels are the first fruits of all the Scriptures, but that of the Gospels that of John is the first fruits. No one can apprehend the meaning of it except he have lain on Jesus' breast and received from Jesus Mary to be his mother also.
lines.ctx: Opening his great commentary on John's Gospel, written for his friend Ambrose.
lines.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
lines.source: Allan Menzies, ANF 9 (1896); survives in Greek
lines.note: New Advent URL for Commentary on John Book 1 not fetched (could_not_verify); CCEL ANF 9 is the checked text.

lines.exact: Be not satisfied with knocking and seeking; for prayer is of all things indispensable to the knowledge of the things of God.
lines.display: Be not satisfied with knocking and seeking; for prayer is of all things indispensable to the knowledge of the things of God.
lines.ctx: To his former pupil Gregory, later the Wonderworker, on how to read the Bible.
lines.source: Crombie, ANF 4 (1885); survives in Greek in the Philocalia
lines.note: Menzies's ANF 9 version (New Advent 1014) words it differently; this line is Crombie's (not on New Advent). If New Advent must be the link, use Menzies's wording instead; check it first.

lines.exact: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars?
lines.display: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars?
lines.ctx: On Genesis 1. He argues that some Bible passages point past the letter to a hidden meaning.
lines.note: Modern editions number this 4.3.1. New Advent has soft hyphens inside 'suppose' and 'existed' (the research note); stripped before checking.

lines.exact: For the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification.
lines.display: For the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification.
lines.ctx: Three sections later, to anyone who thought he doubted the Bible's history.
lines.note: Rufinus's Latin version of the same sentence reads 'For the passages which hold good in their historical acceptation are much more numerous than those which contain a purely spiritual meaning.' Both are on the New Advent page.

lines.exact: that alone is to be accepted as truth which differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.
lines.display: That alone is to be accepted as truth which differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.
lines.ctx: The rule he set himself at the start of his boldest book.
lines.note: Latin only (Rufinus). Crombie's CCEL text reads 'apostolical tradition'; New Advent 'apostolic'.

lines.exact: When a temptation comes which is not in our power to avoid, we must endure it with exceeding nobleness and courage; but, when it is in our power to avoid it, not to do so is rash.
lines.display: When a temptation comes which is not in our power to avoid, we must endure it with exceeding nobleness and courage; but, when it is in our power to avoid it, not to do so is rash.
lines.ctx: On Jesus withdrawing from Herod. Written by a man who as a boy had run toward martyrdom, and who moved from house to house to escape arrest.

lines.exact: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
lines.display: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
lines.ctx: His one surviving sentence from the letter he sent his father in prison, as a boy.
lines.work: Letter to his father (lost), quoted by Eusebius
lines.note: McGiffert's footnote: the letter 'is now lost, and we possess only this sentence from it'.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: He rejected it by name, calling it 'the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God, and not handed down by the Apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures'. What he did teach, and what was later condemned, is that souls existed before birth. That is a different idea.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God, and not handed down by the Apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures
misquoted_or_legend.source: Commentary on Matthew, Book 13, section 1 (tr. John Patrick, ANF 9); Fifth Council, fifteen anathemas, anathema 1 ('the fabulous pre-existence of souls')
misquoted_or_legend.note: The popular add-on 'a council removed reincarnation from the Bible' has no basis in the council texts read (NPNF2-14); not worth printing unless it is searched.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Origen said even the devil would be saved.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: In his lifetime he denied it angrily, calling it 'a thing which not even a madman can say'. His critics still drew it from his system. Augustine, two centuries later, believed he taught it.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: namely, that the father of wickedness and perdition of those who shall be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved; a thing which not even a madman can say.
misquoted_or_legend.source: His letter to friends at Alexandria, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, section 18; Augustine, City of God, Book 21, chapter 17 ('he believed that even the devil himself and his angels ... should be delivered from their torments')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Britannica says in the Candidus debate 'Origen replied that if Satan fell by will, even he can repent'. So: disputed, and the page should say both. Augustine's words checked in augustine-city-of-god-11-23-and-21-17-npnf102.txt.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Jerome himself (Apology 2.19) read the debate with Candidus and says Origen argued the devil "by his own will ... fell and can be saved". The page now uses that primary source in place of Britannica.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: An opponent claimed to have read 6,000 of his books. Jerome, himself no friend of Origen's teaching, called it a lie: Eusebius's list of Origen's works came to 'not a third of that number'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: Count up the index contained in the third volume of Eusebius, in which is his life of Pamphilus: you will not find, I do not say six thousand, but not a third of that number of books.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, section 22 (and Jerome, Letter 84, section 8)
misquoted_or_legend.note: The claim was reported by Rufinus about Epiphanius (the 'one of them' in Jerome's quotation of Rufinus). Epiphanius's own Panarion (copyrighted English) was not read.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Origen was condemned as a heretic in his own lifetime.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: His own bishop had him expelled and deposed, but over his ordination outside Alexandria, not his teaching. Jerome says Rome joined in 'not ... because of the novelty or heterodoxy of his doctrines'. The condemnations of his ideas came after his death, the last in the 540s and 550s.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: not--as the rabid hounds who now pursue him cry--because of the novelty or heterodoxy of his doctrines, but because men could not tolerate the incomparable eloquence and knowledge which, when once he opened his lips, made others seem dumb.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Jerome, Letter 33, section 4; Photius, codex 118 (the decisions were over the ordination); Catholic Encyclopedia ('St. Jerome declares expressly that he was not condemned on a point of doctrine')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Jerome wrote Letter 33 about 384, before he turned against Origen.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Britannica says Demetrius was also "appalled" by Origen's view that even Satan could repent and so "instigated a synodical condemnation"; NPNF's note on Letter 33 says "He appears to have been excommunicated as a heretic". The flat "over his ordination, not his teaching" was one-sided. Page now gives Jerome's view as Jerome's, with Britannica beside it.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Origen read the whole Bible as allegory and did not believe its history.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: He said the opposite: passages true as history are 'much more numerous' than those with only a spiritual meaning. He did think some passages, such as days before the sun, could not be literal.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: For the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification.
misquoted_or_legend.source: On First Principles, Book 4, chapter 1, section 19 (from the Greek)
misquoted_or_legend.note: A common charge in popular writing; the pagan Porphyry already mocked his allegories (Eusebius 6.19.4-8).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He castrated himself (told as settled fact).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Only Eusebius tells it. He calls it the act of 'an immature and youthful mind', done because Origen read Jesus's words on eunuchs too literally. Some modern historians doubt it: Britannica says the story 'may merely have been hostile gossip'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: a deed was done by him which evidenced an immature and youthful mind, but at the same time gave the highest proof of faith and continence.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 8; Britannica, 'Origen'
misquoted_or_legend.note: A hard topic, not a misquote: consider it for 'What was he like' or 'His life' instead, stated plainly. Origen's own later rejection of the literal reading (Commentary on Matthew, Book 15) is not in a public-domain English translation (ANF 9 has Books 1, 2 and 10 to 14 only); could_not_verify.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'Gregory of Nazianzus called Origen "the whetstone of us all".'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The line comes from the Suda, a Byzantine lexicon of about 1000, not from any work of Gregory's we could check. What Gregory certainly did: with Basil the Great he compiled the Philocalia, an anthology of Origen, and sent a copy to a friend as an Easter gift.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: we send you the volume of the Philocalia of Origen, containing a selection of passages useful to students of literature.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (cites 'Suidas, "Lexicon" ... Origenes he panton hemon achone'); Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115 (NPNF2-7)
misquoted_or_legend.note: PARTLY VERIFIED: that the Suda is the only source is from the Catholic Encyclopedia's citation; I did not search all of Gregory's works for the phrase. Use with 'is only known from the Suda' softened to 'comes to us through the Suda'.
misquoted_or_legend.claim_verified: partly: the Philocalia letter is checked word for word; 'the line is known only from the Suda' rests on the Catholic Encyclopedia's citation
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: the Easter date is the NPNF editor's "about Easter a.d. 382". Page: "About Easter 382".

misquoted_or_legend.truth: No church counts him a saint (see 'Is he a saint?'). His father Leonides and several of his pupils are saints; he is not.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Roman Martyrology (1916), 22 April and 28 June; OCA; Coptic Synaxarium 12 Baba

where_he_stood.text: Eight of his 11 recorded positions show a line (three are hidden: anger, mystery, pure). Each line was found word for word in the text named, at the place given. Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.origen.cells).

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.line: The children of the philosophers speak of geometry and music and grammar and rhetoric and astronomy as being ancillary to philosophy; and in the same way we might speak of philosophy itself as being ancillary to Christianity.
rows.note: Menzies's version, not Crombie's (ANF 4 words the letter differently). Found in both CCEL ANF 9 and New Advent 1014.

rows.statement: Lying can be the right thing to do if it protects someone.
rows.line: But a man on whom necessity imposes the responsibility of lying is bound to use very great care, and to use falsehood as he would a stimulant or a medicine.
rows.work: Stromateis (Miscellanies), Book 6, lost; quoted by Jerome
rows.place: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 18
rows.note: The site cuts the sentence with a full stop; it goes on ', and strictly to preserve its measure'. Jerome quotes it to attack Origen ('His teaching is that the master may lie, but the disciple must not'); a hostile witness, which the page can say.

rows.statement: God still speaks to people through dreams.
rows.line: Many have been converted to Christianity as if against their will, some sort of spirit having suddenly transformed their minds from a hatred of the doctrine to a readiness to die in its defense, and having appeared to them either in a waking vision or a dream of the night.
rows.note: CCEL's Crombie spells 'defence'; New Advent 'defense' (the site's form). Next sentence: 'Many such instances have we known'.

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.line: They expel evil spirits, and perform many cures, and foresee certain events.
rows.note: The sentence continues ', according to the will of the Logos.' The subject is 'traces of that Holy Spirit' preserved 'among Christians'.

rows.statement: In many Bible stories, the deeper meaning matters more than the history.
rows.line: I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally.
rows.place: Book 4, chapter 1, section 16 (the Greek text of the Philocalia; 4.3.1 in modern editions)
rows.note: In New Advent's 'Translated from the Greek' section, so Origen's own words, not Rufinus's.

rows.statement: If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to.
rows.line: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
rows.work: Letter to his father Leonides, as Eusebius records it

rows.statement: A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience.
rows.line: We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army — an army of piety — by offering our prayers to God.
rows.note: 'him' is the emperor. CCEL prints '--an army of piety--'; the site's spaced em dashes are a typographic change (VERIFY.md records it).

rows.statement: In the end, God will save everyone.
rows.line: But our belief is, that the Word shall prevail over the entire rational creation, and change every soul into His own perfection.
rows.note: The site stops at 'perfection'; the sentence goes on '; in which state every one, by the mere exercise of his power, will choose what he desires'. Same chapter: whether evil could arise again 'is beyond our present purpose to say'. This hope is what later councils condemned in its fuller form (the 'restoration'), so the page should say so.

friends_family_rivals.name: Leonides
friends_family_rivals.text: Taught him Scripture as a boy and died a martyr in 202. The Roman Martyrology keeps him as a saint on 22 April.

friends_family_rivals.name: His mother
friends_family_rivals.text: Unnamed in the sources. She hid his clothes to stop him running to martyrdom.

friends_family_rivals.name: Clement of Alexandria
friends_family_rivals.text: Eusebius says Origen studied under Clement as a boy, and Photius that he succeeded him as head of the school.
friends_family_rivals.source: Eusebius 6.6; Photius, codex 118; Jerome, Lives 54 ('successor to the presbyter Clement')

friends_family_rivals.name: Ammonius Saccas
friends_family_rivals.text: The pagan philosopher Porphyry says Origen attended the lectures of Ammonius, the founder of the Neoplatonist school.

friends_family_rivals.name: Demetrius of Alexandria
friends_family_rivals.text: Put him in charge of the school and praised him, then turned on him after his ordination and 'wrote everywhere to injure his reputation'. The Coptic Church honours Demetrius as a saint.
friends_family_rivals.source: Eusebius 6.8; Jerome, Lives 54; Coptic Synaxarium, 12 Baba

friends_family_rivals.name: Heraclas
friends_family_rivals.text: One of his first pupils; Origen made him his assistant. Heraclas took over the school when Origen left and succeeded Demetrius as bishop. Britannica says he ended by refusing communion with Origen.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: the 1911 Catholic Encyclopedia says "There is no proof that Heracles ... wavered in his sworn friendship", against Britannica. Both now on the page.

friends_family_rivals.name: Ambrose
friends_family_rivals.text: A rich convert Origen won from the Valentinian sect. He paid for Origen's secretaries and pressed him to write; Against Celsus and the Commentary on John were written for him.

friends_family_rivals.name: Alexander of Jerusalem and Theoctistus of Caesarea
friends_family_rivals.text: They let him preach as a layman, ordained him, and sat under his teaching 'as their only teacher'.

friends_family_rivals.name: Gregory Thaumaturgus (the Wonderworker)
friends_family_rivals.text: Studied under him at Caesarea for five years and left a farewell speech in his praise. Origen's letter to Gregory survives.

friends_family_rivals.name: Julius Africanus
friends_family_rivals.text: Wrote to him that the story of Susanna in Daniel was a later forgery; Origen wrote a long, courteous reply defending it.

friends_family_rivals.name: Mammaea
friends_family_rivals.text: Sent soldiers to bring him to Antioch so she could hear him.

friends_family_rivals.name: Celsus
friends_family_rivals.text: A 2nd-century pagan whose attack on Christianity Origen answered, point by point, in eight books.

friends_family_rivals.name: Porphyry
friends_family_rivals.text: The pagan philosopher met him as a young man, and later mocked his allegorical reading of the Bible.

friends_family_rivals.name: Pamphilus
friends_family_rivals.text: A priest of Caesarea, later martyred, who collected Origen's books and wrote a Defence of Origen in prison with Eusebius.

friends_family_rivals.name: Jerome
friends_family_rivals.text: Called him 'the greatest teacher of the Churches next to the Apostles', translated his homilies, then turned: 'I have praised the commentator but not the theologian.'
friends_family_rivals.source: Jerome, Preface to Hebrew Names; Letter 84, section 2

friends_family_rivals.name: Rufinus
friends_family_rivals.text: Translated On First Principles into Latin and admitted smoothing passages he thought corrupted; fell out bitterly with Jerome over it.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Rufinus's own preface (De Principiis, Book 3, New Advent 04123) says he did "not translate what appeared contrary to Origen's other opinions, and to our own belief, but to pass by such passages as being interpolated and forged by others": he left passages out, he did not say he smoothed them. Page reworded and cited to the preface.

friends_family_rivals.name: Augustine
friends_family_rivals.text: Never met him, but judged the Church right to condemn his idea that even the devil would be freed.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: "two centuries later" was loose (City of God Book 21 is from the 420s, about 170 years after). Page: "Writing in the 420s".

friends_family_rivals.name: Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus
friends_family_rivals.text: Compiled the Philocalia, an anthology of his writings.
friends_family_rivals.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115; Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Letter 115 records one copy sent to one friend, "about Easter a.d. 382" (the editor's date, not Gregory's words). Page: "sent a copy to a friend as a gift" and "About Easter 382".

how_he_died.text: In the persecution of Decius (250) he was imprisoned and tortured: the iron collar, the dungeon, days in the stocks, threats of fire. His judge tried hard to keep him alive. He survived, wrote letters of comfort, and died a few years later at Tyre, aged 69, when Gallus was emperor. He was buried at Tyre. No last words are recorded.
how_he_died.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.39.5 and 7.1; Jerome, Lives 54
how_he_died.note: Photius (codex 118) reports another account from 'Pamphilus the martyr and many others': that he 'quitted this life by a glorious martyrdom at Caesarea' under Decius. Photius thinks the Tyre account truer 'unless the letters supposed to have been written by him after the Decian persecution are spurious'. Print it as 'Another account'. Later: his tomb behind the high altar of Tyre's cathedral (Catholic Encyclopedia; Britannica) is a later tradition; mark it so.

exact_quotes.exact: and how his sufferings terminated, as his judge strove eagerly with all his might not to end his life
At this time Origen died, being sixty-nine years of age.
He lived until the time of Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until his sixty-ninth year, and died at Tyre, in which city he also was buried.
assert that he quitted this life by a glorious martyrdom at Caesarea during the cruel persecution of the Christians by the emperor Decius.

how_he_died.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: Eusebius 6.39.5 says "his feet stretched four spaces in the stocks", not his legs. Page: "his feet were stretched wide in the stocks".

is_he_a_saint.text: No. No church counts him a saint. He was never condemned in his lifetime for his teaching, and many great saints admired him. But from the 390s his ideas were attacked, and in the 540s and 550s the pre-existence of souls and a final 'restoration' of all things were condemned under the emperor Justinian, with Origen named among heretics in the Fifth Council's eleventh anathema (553). Scholars still argue over how much of what was condemned he actually taught.

items.text: Not in the Roman Martyrology. The early 'Gelasian Decree' lists his works among those not received. In strict Catholic usage he is an 'ecclesiastical writer' rather than a Father. Benedict XVI gave two talks praising him (2007).
items.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Fathers of the Church' (1909) and 'Origen and Origenism' (1911); Benedict XVI, General Audiences of 25 April and 2 May 2007 (vatican.va)

items.text: The OCA says the Fifth Ecumenical Council 'examined the errors of presbyter Origen' and condemned his teaching on the pre-existence of souls.
items.source: OCA, Commemoration of the 165 Fathers of the Fifth Ecumenical Council; OCA, The Orthodox Faith vol. III

items.text: The Coptic Synaxarium honours the bishop who excommunicated him.
Not in the Church of England's calendar, the Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, or the Missouri Synod's list.

exact_quotes.exact: If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches and Origen, as well as their impious writings
exact_quotes.note: Percival's excursus (NPNF2-14): some scholars (Halloix, Garnier, Vincenzi) thought Origen's name a later insertion; Hefele keeps it. The fifteen anathemas 'against Origen' may belong to a Constantinople synod of 543, not the council itself: disputed.

exact_quotes.exact: If anyone asserts the fabulous pre-existence of souls, and shall assert the monstrous restoration which follows from it:  let him be anathema.
But the Church, not without reason, condemned him for this and other errors

exact_quotes.who: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), on whether the council itself condemned him
exact_quotes.exact: Were Origen and Origenism anathematized? Many learned writers believe so; an equal number deny that they were condemned; most modern authorities are either undecided or reply with reservations.
exact_quotes.note: PD (1911). Its conclusion: the fifteen anathemas were signed by bishops before the council opened, an 'extra-conciliary sentence' later mistaken for the council's.

exact_quotes.who: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (Episcopal), in Clement's entry
exact_quotes.exact: His work prepared the way for his pupil Origen, the most eminent theologian of early Greek Christianity.
exact_quotes.note: Copyright Church Publishing; a short quotation only.

is_he_a_saint.note: Benedict XVI's audiences (2007) are copyright Libreria Editrice Vaticana; cite, do not quote at length. Text on disk: benedict-xvi-audience-2007-04-25.txt and -05-02.txt.
is_he_a_saint.checker_note: Adversarial check 2026-09-25: "From the 390s his ideas came under attack" missed the earlier critics; the 1911 Catholic Encyclopedia names St Methodius, "bishop and martyr (311)", who wrote several works against Origen. Page adds him.

prayer_he_wrote.text: None found in a public-domain English translation. Leave the section out.
prayer_he_wrote.source: Searched Crombie (ANF 4), Menzies and Patrick (ANF 9) for prayers in his own voice
prayer_he_wrote.note: Against Celsus ends, in Crombie's printing, with 'Glory Be to Thee, Our God; Glory Be to Thee.' It is set as a closing doxology and may be a scribe's, not Origen's; not usable without checking the Greek (could_not_verify). His treatise On Prayer has no public-domain English translation on CCEL or New Advent that was checked.

what_to_read_first.title: Church History, Book 6
what_to_read_first.text: Almost everything we know of his life. Eusebius collected his letters and spoke with people who knew him.
what_to_read_first.note: HTTP 200, title 'Church History, Book VI'. CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf201.iii.xi.html (200).

what_to_read_first.title: Against Celsus
what_to_read_first.text: His answer to a pagan's attack on Christianity, in eight books. Complete in his own Greek.

what_to_read_first.text: His boldest book. Mostly in Rufinus's Latin, which softened it.

hard_topics.text: Eusebius says that as a young teacher he took Matthew 19:12 literally and castrated himself, partly so no one could slander his teaching of women. Eusebius calls it immature but a proof of faith; his bishop first admired it, then used it against him. Britannica says it may be hostile gossip.

Pre-existence of souls and a final restoration of all (including demons) were condemned under Justinian (543 and 553). Origen is named in the Fifth Council's eleventh anathema. Defenders then and now say later 'Origenists' went far beyond him, and that Rufinus's Latin and his enemies' quotations make his real views hard to fix.
hard_topics.source: NPNF2-14; Catholic Encyclopedia; Britannica ('The polemical anti-Origenists ... were not above misquoting Origen and ascribing to him the words of later Origenists')

hard_topics.text: His hope that the Word would win over every soul (Against Celsus 8.72) is the plain-words heart of what later was condemned in fuller form. Augustine calls it an error the Church rightly condemned.

hub_card.note: The hints are right. Not 'teachers' (that collection is 'Great teachers of East and West', i.e. the Doctors: Basil, Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory). Not 'martyrs': he was tortured but did not die of it by the preferred account (Pamphilus's martyrdom claim, via Photius, is the minority account). East: he wrote in Greek at Alexandria and Caesarea, though he visited Rome (Eusebius 6.14.10). Card status line: 'Church Father. Not counted a saint.'

The Suda's 'whetstone of us all' line: known here only through the Catholic Encyclopedia's citation; Gregory of Nazianzus's own works were not searched for it.
The closing doxology of Against Celsus ('Glory Be to Thee, Our God; Glory Be to Thee.'): may be scribal; the Greek was not checked.
Origen's own rejection of a literal reading of Matthew 19:12 (Commentary on Matthew, Book 15): no public-domain English translation (ANF 9 stops at Book 14).

numbers.chip: Age when his father was martyred
numbers.evidence: Eusebius, Church History 6.2.12 (sources/people/origen/eusebius-church-history-book6.txt line ~152): 'he was left with his mother and six younger brothers when he was not quite seventeen years old.' Year 202: Britannica (britannica-origen.txt line 328): 'Origen's father, Leonides, was martyred in 202'. The quoted line is already in origen.quotes.json.

Eusebius, Church History 6.23.2 (eusebius-church-history-book6.txt line 3422): 'For he dictated to more than seven amanuenses, who relieved each other at appointed times. And he employed no fewer copyists, besides girls who were skilled in elegant writing. For all these Ambrose furnished the necessary expense in abundance'.
lines_now: More than seven, taking turns as he spoke
No fewer copyists, all paid for by his patron Ambrose
numbers.checker_note: Second line was 'As many copyists too, all paid for by his friend Ambrose'. Now Eusebius's own 'no fewer', and 'patron' as the trait and the circle call him (so no one takes him for Ambrose of Milan).

numbers.evidence: Britannica (britannica-origen.txt line 421): 'The Hexapla was a synopsis of Old Testament versions: the Hebrew and a transliteration, the Septuagint ..., the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion ... The purpose of the Hexapla was to provide a secure basis for debate with rabbis to whom the Hebrew alone was authoritative.' Hebrew + transliteration + four Greek versions = six. Eusebius 6.16 (line ~1992) for the Hexapla itself. The Hebrew 'in Greek letters' (Britannica says only 'a transliteration'): ANF 4, introductory note to Origen (sources/people/origen/anf04-origen-introductory-note.txt lines 593-594): 'In the first was placed the current Hebrew text; in the second, the same represented in Greek letters'; also Benedict XVI, audience of 25 April 2007 (benedict-xvi-audience-2007-04-25.txt line 110): 'the Hebrew text transliterated into Greek characters, and then four different translations in Greek'.

tidbits.text: The boy's questions, and his father kissing his chest
tidbits.evidence: Eusebius, Church History 6.2.9-11 (eusebius-church-history-book6.txt lines 133-147): 'he puzzled his father with inquiries for the true meaning of the inspired Scriptures' ... 'And they say that often, standing by the boy when asleep, he uncovered his breast as if the Divine Spirit were enshrined within it, and kissed it reverently'. Not elsewhere on the page (Grew up has only the daily recitation, 6.2.8).
tidbits.text_now: As a boy he puzzled his father with questions about the deeper meaning of Scripture. The story went that his father would stand over the sleeping boy, bare his chest and kiss it, as if the Spirit of God lived there.
tidbits.checker_note: Eusebius gives the kiss as hearsay ('And they say that often ...'), so the line now says 'The story went', not a flat statement.

tidbits.text: Jerome: on the Song of Songs he outdid himself
tidbits.evidence: Jerome, Preface to the Translation of Origen's Two Homilies on the Song of Songs, NPNF 2.6 (jerome-preface-origen-song-of-songs-npnf206.txt line 28-29): 'Origen, whilst in his other books he has surpassed all others, has in the Song of Songs surpassed himself. He wrote ten volumes upon it'. Free copy: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf206.vii.ii.ii.html (checked 2026-09-25).

tidbits.text: Every philosopher and poet, except the atheists
tidbits.evidence: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen, Argument 13 (gregory-thaumaturgus-panegyric-on-origen-anf06.txt lines 1270-1280): 'he deemed it right for us to study philosophy in such wise, that we should read with utmost diligence all that has been written, both by the philosophers and by the poets of old, rejecting nothing ... except only the productions of the atheists, who ... deny that there is either a God or a providence. From these he would have us abstain, because they are not worthy of being read'.
